objective: Performing a P5 Impact Analysis: Product lenses (lifespan, servicing) and Process lenses (efficiency, effectiveness, fairness)
secondaryObjectives: Evaluating People impacts: labor practices and decent work, community/customer concerns, human rights considerations, and ethical behavior (anti-corruption, greenwashing)
Evaluating Planet and Prosperity impacts: transport/consumption considerations, project feasibility (business case, social ROI), business agility, and market/economic stimulation
Evaluating P5 Impact Analysis results: analysis mechanics, assigning items to elements, and project status reporting at closure

sources.cite: PMI, Certified Sustainable Project Professional (CSPP) bundle and exam page: P5 Standard: Sustainability and Impact Analysis 24% (the largest domain with PRiSM Life Cycle Approach 23% and Project Management Considerations 23%)
sources.note: Read 2026-11-17 directly (summarizing fetch of pmi.org/certifications/cspp-bundle-exam-course). The page lists six domains: Foundations of Sustainable Project Work 12%, PRiSM Life Cycle Approach 23%, P5 Standard: Sustainability and Impact Analysis 24%, Developing a Sustainability Management Plan 12%, ESG & Sustainability Reporting, Governance, and Project Communications 7%, Project Management Considerations 23% (they add to 101%). It says the P5 Standard evaluates project impacts on 'people, planet, and prosperity', and a prep module practices 'a P5 Impact Analysis' to 'identify, assess and mitigate sustainability impacts'. The course seed's five domains and weights (P5 36%) differ from this page; the P5 domain is the largest either way. The objective wording is the course seed's.

sources.cite: GPM Global, The GPM P5 Standard for Sustainability in Project Management, version 2.0 (September 2019; patch releases 2.0.1 and 2.0.2, February 2020)
sources.note: Read 2026-11-17 through a summarizing fetch of a copy of the PDF hosted by a third party. Categories: Product (lifespan, servicing of the product); Process (effectiveness, efficiency and fairness of project processes); People (labor practices and decent work, society and customers, human rights, ethical behavior including procurement practices and anti-corruption); Planet (transport, energy, land, air and water, consumption including recycling and reuse, disposal, contamination and pollution, waste generation); Prosperity (business case analysis, business agility, economic stimulation). The P5 Impact Analysis starts as early as possible and is updated regularly: identify events for each element, describe causes and potential impacts, rate each impact by 'the magnitude of their effect on sustainability', identify responses that minimize negative and maximize positive impacts, and re-rate assuming the response is implemented; an item may be recorded under several elements. The standard sets no numeric scale.
The school district, the offers, the prices, device lifespans, the recyclers and the support gauges are fictional teaching figures for exam practice, not measured values.

brief.situation: You are the project manager for Pine Hollow Unified, a fictional school district, replacing 2,000 student laptops before the next school year. The district's sustainability policy asks every capital project to analyze and report its impacts. The budget is 1,600 thousand dollars.
handover: Three offers are due in week 4; 2,000 old laptops must leave the schools by week 8.
The school board approves the announcement; the teachers' association and a parents' group sit on the project's advisory group.
howItWorks: The board shows the project's impact register against the district's appetite, each group's support in words, the budget committed and the docket.
Move on two weeks at a time. A decision comes to you at each review; before the first you can compare the offers over six years or check the recyclers.
After week 10 you write the closing status of the impact analysis and a short reflection.

p5Prompt.title: Week 2: the project's sustainability impacts
p5Prompt.context: The district's sustainability policy asks every capital project for an impact analysis at the start. The supplier's sales lead says its products 'are sustainable' and offers to fill in the form.

choices.label: Run a P5 impact analysis with teachers, IT, finance and a parents' group: for each element, the events, causes and impacts, rated, with responses and a re-rating; include the rollout order (schools with the most failed devices first) as a process-fairness item

effects.log: Impacts rated across product, process, people, planet and prosperity; the largest are device lifespan, disposal, and which schools wait longest.

choices.feedback: A P5 impact analysis covers every element, rates each impact, sets responses and re-rates; it is done by the project, early, with stakeholders.

choices.label: Estimate the new laptops' energy use; that is the environmental question
choices.feedback: Energy is one Planet element; lifespan, servicing, disposal, labor and fairness are left out.

choices.label: Let the supplier fill in the sustainability form
choices.feedback: The project owns its impact analysis; a vendor's self-description is not one.

offerPrompt.title: Week 4: three offers
offerPrompt.context: A: 640 dollars a laptop, three-year expected life, battery glued in, no parts after two years. B: 690 dollars, five to six years, battery and keyboard replaceable by district IT, parts for six years. C: offer A plus 20 dollars of carbon offsets each, sold as 'carbon neutral'.

choices.label: Award offer B: over six years it is bought once, serviced in-house, and its cost is about 1,460 thousand dollars against about 2,560 for A

effects.log: Offer B awarded; district IT is trained on battery and keyboard swaps.

choices.feedback: The Product lenses weigh lifespan and servicing; a longer-lived, repairable device lowers both impact and the cost over the period.

choices.label: Award offer A: lowest price, within budget
choices.feedback: The lowest price buys the devices twice in six years and leaves broken ones unrepairable.

choices.label: Award offer C and use its 'carbon neutral' label in the district's report
choices.feedback: Offsets do not change the product's lifespan or servicing; the label invites a claim the project cannot support.

dispPrompt.title: Week 6: the 2,000 old laptops
dispPrompt.context: A certified electronics recycler will wipe the drives, refurbish about 600 for families without a computer and recycle the rest with an audited downstream, for a net 40 thousand dollars. A broker bids 10 thousand dollars for the lot, collected as is; it will not say where they go. A warehouse would cost 15 thousand dollars a year.

choices.label: Use the certified recycler: drives wiped, 600 refurbished for families, the rest recycled with an audited downstream

effects.log: Collected; wipe certificates and the downstream audit filed.

choices.feedback: Disposal is a Planet (consumption) and People (human rights, community) impact; a certified, audited downstream and reuse address both.

choices.label: Sell the lot to the broker: it brings in money
choices.feedback: An unknown downstream can mean hand-stripping in unsafe conditions and unwiped student data.

choices.label: Store them in a warehouse until next year
choices.feedback: Storage defers the impact and adds cost; the devices lose reuse value every month.

claimPrompt.title: Week 8: the board's announcement
claimPrompt.context: The communications office drafts: 'Our new zero-impact student devices.' The board meets next week to announce the program.

choices.label: Rewrite it with the analysis: what was rated, what the responses changed, and what impact remains (manufacture and shipping)

effects.log: The announcement reports the impacts as rated, with what remains.

choices.feedback: Sustainability communications report impacts as analyzed, including what remains; an absolute claim is greenwashing.

choices.label: Publish it: the families will like it
choices.feedback: No device has zero impact; the claim cannot be supported by the analysis.

choices.label: Publish nothing about sustainability
choices.feedback: Silence avoids greenwashing but leaves stakeholders without the results they were promised.

reflection.question: Write the closing sustainability note: which impacts the analysis found, what you did about lifespan, servicing, disposal and the claim, and what remains.

parts.label: The analysis
parts.criteria: Covers all five elements early with stakeholders, rates the impacts and re-rates after the responses; names process fairness in the rollout.
parts.modelAnswer: At the start we rated impacts across the five elements with teachers, IT, finance and parents: lifespan, disposal and which schools waited longest were the largest; rollout went to the schools with most failed devices first.

parts.label: Responses and reporting
parts.criteria: The repairable, longer-lived offer; certified disposal with reuse; and an announcement that reports remaining impact without an absolute claim.
parts.modelAnswer: Offer B lasts five to six years and is serviced in-house, about 1,460 thousand dollars over six years against 2,560. The old laptops went to a certified recycler, 600 to families. We reported what remains, manufacture and shipping, rather than 'zero impact'.

scoring.modelReasoning: A P5 impact analysis is the project's own work, done early with stakeholders: for each element, identify events, describe causes and impacts, rate them, set responses and re-rate. Here the Product lenses decide the offer: a repairable laptop that lasts five to six years is bought once and serviced in-house, lowering both impact and the six-year cost; offsets change neither lifespan nor servicing. Disposal is a Planet and People impact: a certified, audited downstream with data wiping and reuse, not the highest bidder. Communications report impacts as analyzed with what remains; 'zero impact' is greenwashing.
